Sequence.title: From Machinery Noise to a Sonar Track
Sequence.headline: Follow the dependency chain that lets a passive array turn pressure fluctuations into a classified contact.
Sequence.kicker: Ocean acoustics laboratory · A distant ship is radiating broadband and tonal sound
story: A ship over the horizon cannot be seen, yet its machinery and propeller disturb the surrounding water. A passive sonar operator receives only the pressure field that survives the ocean path.
Arrange the physical and computational sequence from source vibration to a stable bearing-and-frequency track.
Sequence.overview: Passive sonar does not transmit a pulse. It depends on sound generated by a source, propagation through a variable ocean, conversion of pressure to electrical signals, array processing, and repeated observations that support classification. Each stage needs the output of the stage before it.
terms: Formation and collapse of vapor bubbles near a propeller when local pressure falls sufficiently.
How sound speed changes with depth because of temperature, salinity, and pressure.
Bending of a wave path when propagation speed changes with position.
A sensor that converts underwater pressure changes into an electrical signal.
Combining time-shifted array channels to favor sound arriving from one direction.
A narrow frequency feature often associated with rotating machinery.
A time-linked estimate of a contact’s bearing, motion, and signal features.
Sequence.note: Real oceans can create multiple paths, shadow zones, and strong biological or shipping noise. The game uses a single dominant path so the causal order remains unique.
Sequence.sources: Fact-checked against U.S. Navy and NOAA primers on underwater sound, sound-speed variation, sonar, hydrophones, and acoustic propagation.

cards: Loaded machinery and the propulsion shaft exert changing forces
Those forces vibrate machinery foundations, hull plating, and the propeller
The moving surfaces push and pull on nearby seawater
The resulting pressure disturbances radiate as an acoustic field
Sound energy leaves the source region
The local sound-speed profile sets how rays bend
Spreading and absorption reduce the received level
A weakened pressure pattern reaches the receiving array
Hydrophones convert pressure changes into voltage signals
The processor applies relative delays across array channels
Repeated bearings and spectral lines are associated into a contact track

segues: The source has created a pressure field, but the receiver will not observe a simple copy. The ocean path now determines which frequencies and directions survive.
The array has received pressure fluctuations, not a contact label. Sensor conversion and coherent processing must turn those fluctuations into directional evidence before tracking can begin.
principles: Trace the information carrier
Mechanical vibration becomes pressure variation, then voltage, then a directional estimate.
Propagation happens before detection
The sound-speed structure and transmission loss act on the signal before any processor can recover it.
An array needs relative timing
Direction comes from phase or arrival-time differences among separated hydrophones.
Classification follows detection
A stable bearing and spectrum provide the evidence used to form and classify a track.
hints: The hull must first move the water before any acoustic pressure field can leave the source.
Hydrophones produce channel voltages before beamforming can favor an arrival direction.
Sequence.intro: The distant ship is operating steadily. Sequence A must create an underwater pressure disturbance before ocean propagation or receiver processing can occur.

Sequence.title: From Radar Pulse to Confirmed Track
Sequence.headline: Order the physical and information-processing steps behind pulse-echo radar.
Sequence.kicker: Surface-search radar · A small contact is near the electromagnetic horizon
story: A rotating radar must illuminate a sector, receive a tiny echo amid noise and clutter, and decide whether repeated returns belong to one moving object.
Arrange the chain from waveform creation through detection, ranging, and track formation.
Sequence.overview: Radar range is inferred from elapsed time, but a usable track requires much more than a stopwatch. The transmitter must create a waveform, the antenna must radiate it, the target must scatter some energy back, the receiver must protect itself and recover the echo, and repeated measurements must be associated over time.
terms: A device that alternately connects a shared antenna to the transmitter and receiver while protecting the receiver.
Energy redirected toward the radar after the wave interacts with a target.
A processor designed to maximize response to a known waveform in noise.
A time window corresponding to a selected distance interval.
Unwanted echoes from sea, land, weather, or other distributed reflectors.
A time-linked record of estimated target position and motion.
Sequence.note: Real radars may use pulse compression, Doppler processing, electronic steering, and parallel tracking. The sequence shows the dependency order common to pulse-echo systems.
Sequence.sources: Fact-checked against Naval History and Heritage Command radar descriptions and standard pulse-echo radar principles.

cards: The exciter forms a timed radio-frequency waveform
The transmitter raises the waveform to high peak power
The duplexer connects the antenna to the transmitter
The antenna directs the pulse into a search sector
After the pulse, the duplexer connects the antenna to the protected receiver
The transmitted pulse propagates outward at electromagnetic-wave speed
A target intercepts and backscatters a small fraction
The echo returns through the antenna and receive path
The receiver and matched filter recover echo energy
Round-trip delay is converted into target range
Threshold and clutter processing declare a plot
Plots from successive scans are associated into a track

segues: The pulse has left the antenna. A range measurement is impossible until energy interacts with an object and returns to the same radar.
The receiver now has a weak waveform mixed with noise and clutter. Signal processing must recover evidence from each scan before a tracker can connect detections through time.
principles: Range comes from round-trip time
The clock starts with transmission and ends when the echo is received.
Most transmitted energy never returns
Target geometry and spreading make the received echo far weaker than the outgoing pulse.
Detection is not tracking
One threshold crossing is a plot; motion requires association across scans.
Protection precedes reception
A shared-antenna receiver must be isolated from the high-power transmit pulse.
hints: The target must scatter the outward pulse before an echo can travel back.
A plot must be declared on an individual scan before successive plots can be associated into a track.
Sequence.intro: The radar has not yet transmitted. Sequence A must create, amplify, switch, and radiate a waveform before any target echo can exist.

Sequence.title: From Intake Air to Propeller Thrust
Sequence.headline: Follow energy through a marine gas-turbine propulsion train.
Sequence.kicker: Engineering plant · A gas turbine is ordered from idle to ahead power
story: The bridge requests more speed. Fuel alone cannot turn the propeller: the plant must establish airflow, release heat, extract shaft work, transmit torque, and accelerate water astern.
Arrange the thermodynamic and mechanical chain that produces ship thrust.
Sequence.overview: A marine gas turbine is an open-cycle heat engine. The compressor raises air pressure, fuel adds chemical energy, hot gas expands through turbine stages, and a power turbine drives reduction gearing and a shaft. The propeller then converts shaft torque into a pressure and momentum change in the water.
terms: Rotating stages that raise the pressure of incoming air.
Chamber where fuel burns in compressed air.
Turbine stages that power the compressor.
Turbine that extracts useful output shaft work.
Gearing that trades high turbine speed for lower propeller speed and higher torque.
The geometric advance associated with one propeller revolution in an ideal solid medium.
Force produced by changing the momentum and pressure of a fluid.
Sequence.note: Some ships use controllable-pitch propellers, combining gears, or electric transmission. This sequence follows a direct mechanical gas-turbine drive.
Sequence.sources: Fact-checked against standard Brayton-cycle and marine propulsion descriptions used in naval engineering education.

cards: Intake ducts deliver filtered ambient air
Compressor stages raise the air pressure
Fuel is metered and burns in the compressed airflow
Hot gas expands through the gas-generator turbine
The gas-generator turbine keeps the compressor turning
Remaining gas energy turns the free power turbine
Reduction gearing lowers rotational speed and raises shaft torque
The propulsion shaft carries torque toward the stern
The propeller rotates under applied shaft torque
Blade sections create a pressure difference across the propeller disk
The propeller accelerates a mass of water astern
The reaction force accelerates the ship ahead

segues: The gas generator is now self-sustaining. Useful propulsion still requires extracting remaining exhaust energy on a separate output shaft and matching its speed to the propeller.
Torque has reached the propeller shaft, but torque is not yet ship motion. The propeller must exchange momentum with the water to create an external force on the hull.
principles: Follow energy, not just components
Chemical energy becomes thermal energy, gas kinetic energy, shaft work, and finally fluid momentum.
The compressor must be paid for
Part of turbine work only keeps the engine breathing; useful output comes after that internal demand.
Gearing matches machines
Turbines favor high rotational speed while large propellers operate efficiently at much lower speed.
Thrust requires the environment
The ship moves because the propeller pushes water astern and water pushes the propeller—and ship—ahead.
hints: Compressed air must reach the combustor before fuel can burn stably in the gas path.
Reduction gearing changes turbine speed before torque reaches the propeller shaft.
Sequence.intro: The bridge has requested ahead power, but the engine contains only stationary air and rotating machinery at idle. Sequence A must establish the pressurized hot-gas path.

Sequence.title: From Air Search to Engagement Assessment
Sequence.headline: Order the information and authorization chain in a layered defensive response.
Sequence.kicker: Task-group operations room · An uncorrelated air contact approaches
story: A surveillance sensor reports a new contact. The force must transform an uncertain return into a shared track, assess identity and intent, select a proportionate response, and determine whether the threat remains.
Arrange the high-level decision chain without assuming that detection automatically authorizes engagement.
Sequence.overview: A defensive system is a chain of evidence and control. Sensors create measurements; trackers create state estimates; identification combines cooperative, intelligence, and behavioral evidence; command evaluates rules and risk; weapons or countermeasures require a quality solution; and assessment closes the loop.
terms: A sensor-level observation from one scan or report.
A time-linked estimate of position, velocity, and uncertainty.
Assessment of whether a contact is friendly, neutral, unknown, or hostile.
Determining whether reports from different sensors describe the same object.
Accuracy and update rate sufficient for a selected engagement system.
Command permission under applicable rules and delegated authority.
Evaluation of whether the action achieved the intended effect.
Sequence.note: The puzzle stays at public, system-level concepts. Real engagement criteria, ranges, tactics, and authorities depend on mission and classification.
Sequence.sources: Fact-checked against public naval radar, command-and-control, identification, and layered-defense concepts.

cards: A surveillance sensor generates an uncorrelated plot
Successive plots initiate a tentative track
Other sensor reports are correlated with that track
The fused track gains a better position, velocity, and uncertainty estimate
Cooperative, intelligence, and behavior evidence support identification
Command evaluates intent, rules, geometry, and risk
The force selects a warning, maneuver, countermeasure, or engagement option
The responsible authority approves the selected action
Sensors maintain the quality required by the chosen system
Sensors observe the contact and action effects
The force assesses whether the threat is removed or another layer is required

segues: A common operating picture now contains a refined track. The next dependency is judgment: identity, intent, authority, and proportional response must be established before action.
The action has been authorized. Execution still depends on adequate track quality, and the defensive cycle is not complete until sensors determine what changed.
principles: A measurement is not a decision
Sensor evidence must be tracked, correlated, and interpreted before command action.
Identity and intent are separate questions
A known platform can still behave unexpectedly; an unknown contact is not automatically hostile.
Authority is load-bearing
A technically possible action may remain prohibited or inappropriate.
Assessment closes the loop
Defensive systems must observe outcomes and decide whether another response is needed.
hints: Successive plots must first initiate a track before reports from other sensors can be correlated to it.
Authorization comes before execution, while assessment comes only after effects can be observed.
Sequence.intro: Only one sensor has reported the contact. Sequence A must turn isolated measurements into a refined shared track before identification and command judgment can proceed.

Diagnosis.title: The Water Keeps Rising
Diagnosis.domain: Shipboard damage control and fluid systems
Diagnosis.role: You are the damage-control assistant coordinating the casualty response.

intro.title: Read the whole flooding panel
intro.lead: A rising bilge alarm does not identify its source. Salinity, system pressure, isolation response, tank soundings, pump performance, and list reveal where the water comes from and whether the ship is gaining on it.

cards.title: How water enters
cards.body: Flooding can cross the hull boundary, escape from a pressurized seawater system, move through ballast piping, or only appear to rise because a sensor fails.

cards.title: How systems identify themselves
cards.body: A ruptured pressurized branch loses pressure. A ballast error changes tank inventory. A hull breach ignores isolation of intact ship systems.

cards.title: What dewatering proves
cards.body: Pump discharge confirms real water and establishes whether removal capacity exceeds the ingress rate.

cards.title: Why calm readings matter
cards.body: Normal firemain and cooling pressure can be decisive: they show which plausible seawater sources are not feeding the compartment.

intro.takeaway: Trace the water across boundaries. The correct diagnosis must explain its salinity, rate, pressure signature, valve response, and stability effect at the same time.

parts: Shell plating and sea chests separate the compartment from outside seawater.
A high-pressure seawater network supplies firefighting stations.
Sea-connected pumps and coolers remove heat from equipment.
Valves and tanks intentionally move seawater to control draft, list, and trim.
Level sensors and pumps detect and remove water from normally dry spaces.
system.soWrong: The same rising-level alarm can come from five different physical paths—or no water at all. Pressure, salinity, valve response, tank inventory, and independent level measurements locate the path.

level.name: Machinery-room bilge level
level.purpose: Shows water accumulation in the compartment; a rise may be real ingress or a bad channel.

salinity.name: Bilge conductivity / salinity
salinity.purpose: Distinguishes seawater-like ingress from fresh condensate or a dry sensor alarm.

firemain.name: Firemain pressure
firemain.purpose: Falls when a pressurized firemain branch ruptures or is isolated.

cooling.name: Seawater cooling pressure
cooling.purpose: Falls when the machinery cooling branch loses inventory or pump head.

isolation.name: Isolation response
isolation.purpose: Shows whether closing a named branch stops the ingress rate.

list.name: Ship list
list.purpose: A growing asymmetric flood adds off-center weight; a false level signal does not.

ballast.name: Ballast-tank soundings
ballast.purpose: Reveal commanded or accidental movement of seawater through the ballast system.

pump.name: Bilge-pump discharge
pump.purpose: Confirms whether the pump is moving water and whether ingress exceeds removal.

redundant.name: Independent level channel
redundant.purpose: Confirms a physical water rise independently of the presenting sensor.

adjacent.name: Adjacent compartment boundary
adjacent.purpose: Checks for progressive flooding beyond the initial watertight boundary.

hull.label: Hull breach below the waterline
hull.choice: Seawater enters directly through damaged shell plating and continues despite isolation of intact ship systems.

call.title: Hull breach — set boundaries and patch.
call.arg: Ingress is external to ship piping; control progressive flooding and establish a patch or shoring plan.

firemain.label: Ruptured firemain branch

Casebook.title: The Greywake Shoal
Casebook.subt: A deduction game inside the Greywake grounding inquiry
Casebook.teaser: A destroyer passes dangerously close to a charted shoal after its electronic chart and radar overlay appear to agree. Was the ship deliberately spoofed, carried helplessly by an exceptional current, or guided by a heading error that independent fixes would have exposed?

Casebook.overclaimTease: Compare heading, position, radar range, and current evidence. Spoofing, set and drift, and a common heading-reference error do not disagree in the same channels.

A wrong gyro correction biased the overlay while independent fixes were waived
An exceptional current carried a correctly navigated ship off track

nc_qm.hint: The written night order suspended radar-range and visual-bearing fixes after the overlay was declared reliable.

nc_radar.name: OS2 Malik Chen
nc_radar.hint: Fixed lighthouse ranges drifted away from the chart overlay even while satellite positions remained smooth and internally consistent.

nc_anschutz.lede: The engineer whose north-seeking gyroscope gave steel ships a heading reference independent of magnetic disturbance.
nc_anschutz.profile:
Hermann Anschütz-Kaempfe developed one of the first practical gyrocompasses after recognizing that a magnetic compass could be unreliable near large masses of steel and electrical equipment. A gyrocompass uses a rapidly spinning rotor, Earth rotation, gravity, and controlled damping to settle toward true north rather than magnetic north. Its usefulness is not that it can never be wrong, but that its errors have different causes and can be checked against celestial, visual, magnetic, or inertial references.

A modern bridge may distribute one gyro heading to radar stabilization, an electronic chart, autopilot, and other consumers. That convenience creates a common-mode risk: two displays can agree because they share the same wrong input. Independent evidence must therefore come from a source that does not inherit the same heading reference.

On Greywake, radar video and the electronic-chart overlay appeared aligned because both used the same entered gyro correction. Raw radar ranges to fixed lighthouses did not need that correction and began rejecting the displayed track. The integrated console preserved the misleading agreement while the fix log recorded the missing independent challenge.
nc_anschutz.frame: Points to a compass repeater and two displays fed from the same heading bus. “Agreement is only evidence when the channels are actually independent.”

q.q: Why can a gyrocompass be preferable to a magnetic compass on a steel ship?

o.t: It measures water current directly beneath the hull.
o.fb: A gyrocompass provides heading, not current.

o.t: It seeks true north without relying on Earth’s local magnetic field.
o.fb: Its north reference comes from gyroscopic dynamics, Earth rotation, gravity, and damping.

o.t: It receives true north continuously from navigation satellites.
o.fb: Modern systems may combine sources, but the gyrocompass principle is self-contained.

o.t: It cannot develop systematic error once spun up.
o.fb: Gyrocompasses require correction and comparison; treating them as infallible creates common-mode risk.

clue.label: WHAT — heading reference
clue.text: The maintenance entry applied a 2.8-degree correction with the wrong sign, biasing every display that consumed the gyro heading.

q.q: When radar overlay and electronic chart agree, what must be checked before calling them independent?

o.t: Whether both displays use the same heading, position, or timing input.
o.fb: Shared inputs can create agreement without independent confirmation.

o.t: Whether their screens use the same brightness setting.
o.fb: Brightness affects presentation, not navigation independence.

o.t: Whether both are located on the bridge.
o.fb: Location does not determine whether their data sources are independent.

o.t: Whether the newer display has priority over the older one.
o.fb: Recency is not a substitute for measurement independence.

clue.label: WHERE — common mode
clue.text: The misleading agreement was strongest at the integrated radar–chart console because both layers were stabilized by the same biased gyro input.

q.q: Which observation most directly tests a heading-reference error?

o.t: A larger-than-forecast engine fuel rate.
o.fb: Fuel rate does not directly test heading.

o.t: A smooth satellite-position trace by itself.
o.fb: Position smoothness does not reveal a shared heading bias.

o.t: A difference between gyro heading and an independent visual or celestial azimuth.
o.fb: An external azimuth tests the heading reference without inheriting its error.

o.t: The absence of an equipment alarm.
o.fb: Calibration and sign errors can remain plausible and alarm-free.

clue.label: WHO — authority
clue.text: Lt. Mara Voss signed the order treating the integrated overlay as sufficient and suspending the independent visual-bearing check.

nc_sumner.lede: The sea captain who realized that one celestial observation can define a whole line on which the ship must lie.
nc_sumner.profile:
Thomas Hubbard Sumner’s 1837 Atlantic landfall produced a foundational navigation insight. When uncertain of latitude, he computed several positions from the same celestial observation and found that they lay along a line. The ship did not need a complete position from one measurement; it needed the geometric constraint that the observation actually supplied. Intersections with later or different lines could then fix position.

The deeper lesson survives in radar and electronic navigation. A range to a charted lighthouse defines a circle; a visual bearing defines a line; a depth contour constrains location; a satellite receiver supplies a position estimate. The strongest fix comes from constraints with different error mechanisms and useful crossing geometry.

On Greywake, fixed radar ranges formed circles that moved away from the electronic-chart symbol as the ship approached the shoal. Those ranges did not depend on the entered gyro correction. The navigation officer’s order removed the very observations that would have forced the integrated display to answer an independent geometric question.
nc_sumner.frame: Draws a range circle crossing a bearing line. “A fix is not a decorated dot. It is the intersection of constraints that could disagree.”

q.q: What is a line of position?

o.t: A route the ship has been ordered to follow.
o.fb: A planned track is not a measured positional constraint.

o.t: A set of possible positions consistent with one observation.
o.fb: One observation often constrains position to a line or curve rather than a single point.

o.t: The line connecting two satellites in orbit.
o.fb: Satellite geometry is different from the navigation meaning.

o.t: A guarantee that every instrument agrees.
o.fb: A line of position is useful precisely because it can challenge other evidence.

clue.label: WHERE — independent geometry
clue.text: Raw radar ranges to two fixed lighthouses rejected the ship symbol at the radar–electronic chart integration console.

q.q: Why are two differently generated lines of position valuable?

o.t: Their intersection can locate the ship while exposing incompatible measurements.
o.fb: Independent constraints produce a fix and reveal disagreement.

o.t: They allow the navigator to average away any large mistake automatically.
o.fb: Averaging can hide a systematic error instead of diagnosing it.

o.t: They make current and wind physically disappear.
o.fb: Environmental forces remain; fixes only measure their effect.

o.t: They ensure the ship follows the planned course between fixes.
o.fb: They reveal position at observation times, not automatic compliance between them.

clue.label: WHAT — cross-check
clue.text: The fix log shows that radar-range and visual-bearing lines were omitted after the integrated overlay was declared reliable.

q.q: Who is accountable for deciding whether the fix method is sufficient?

o.t: Only the radar manufacturer.
o.fb: Equipment design does not replace shipboard navigation authority.

o.t: The person at the helm, regardless of orders.
o.fb: The helmsman executes steering but does not own the fix policy.

o.t: The navigation officer who approves the fix interval and independent sources.
o.fb: The policy decision belongs to the officer responsible for the navigation plan and team.

o.t: No one, because electronic charts are self-validating.
o.fb: Electronic presentation cannot validate its own shared inputs.

clue.label: WHO — fix policy
clue.text: Lt. Mara Voss approved the night order that replaced independent fixes with confidence in the common display.

nc_maury.topic: Winds, currents, and evidence at sea
nc_maury.lede: The U.S. naval officer who turned thousands of ship logs into systematic wind and current charts.
nc_maury.profile:
Matthew Fontaine Maury organized observations from ships’ logs to map prevailing winds and currents, showing that scattered operational records could become a predictive science. His charts shortened voyages by helping mariners choose routes that worked with recurring environmental patterns rather than treating the ocean as featureless.

A current forecast is not a command to believe a number. It is a prior estimate to be updated with measured set and drift. Navigators compare predicted motion through the water with observed motion over the ground, then determine how much cross-track displacement the current can physically accumulate over time.

On Greywake, the embarked oceanographer measured a cross-current stronger than the forecast but not remotely large enough to create the full error. Integrating the measured current over the interval accounted for 0.8 nautical mile of set; the ship missed the intended track by 2.7 nautical miles. Current mattered, but it could not rescue the claim that the navigation references were correct.
nc_maury.frame: Places a current vector beside a longer observed displacement. “An environmental explanation must pay the full distance budget, not merely point in the right direction.”

q.q: What made Maury’s wind and current work scientifically useful?

o.t: He replaced observations with one universal ocean model.
o.fb: His contribution depended on aggregating many observations, not ignoring them.

o.t: He compiled repeated ship reports into patterns that could be tested and used.
o.fb: Systematic aggregation made environmental regularities operationally useful.

o.t: He proved currents never vary from their averages.
o.fb: Charts describe patterns and variability, not immutable flow.

o.t: He invented the gyrocompass.
o.fb: His work concerned oceanography and route planning, not gyrocompass engineering.

clue.label: WHAT — distance budget
clue.text: Measured current integrated over the interval accounts for about 0.8 nautical mile, while the observed cross-track error reached 2.7 nautical miles.

q.q: How should a navigator test whether current explains an off-track position?

o.t: Check whether the current direction is vaguely toward the error.
o.fb: Direction alone does not establish sufficient magnitude.

o.t: Multiply measured drift by exposure time and compare the resulting displacement with the full error.
o.fb: The environmental cause must close the quantitative displacement budget.

o.t: Assume the largest forecast value occurred for the entire watch.
o.fb: Choosing an extreme without measurement can manufacture an explanation.

o.t: Ignore current whenever satellite navigation is available.
o.fb: Current still determines motion over ground and should be measured or estimated.

clue.label: WHERE — measured environment
clue.text: The ocean forecast desk recorded a real but insufficient current; the unresolved discrepancy remained visible at the navigation console.

q.q: Which decision turned a manageable environmental uncertainty into a near grounding?

o.t: The helmsman held the ordered heading.
o.fb: The helmsman followed the command and could not see the full reference problem.

o.t: The technician documented the maintenance action.
o.fb: The sign error began there, but independent fixes could still have caught it.

o.t: The navigation officer waived the independent fixes that would separate current from reference error.
o.fb: That policy allowed a correctable discrepancy to persist.

o.t: No decision; current makes precise navigation impossible.
o.fb: Measured current and independent fixes make the uncertainty manageable.

clue.label: WHO — persistence
clue.text: Lt. Mara Voss retained the no-fix order after the first radar-range discrepancy was reported.

story: Greywake did not lose every navigation source. It lost the habit of making them disagree productively.
QM1 Ward holds the fix log and night orders. OS2 Chen has the radar-range history. Dr. Ortiz has the current observations.
A spoofing attack, an exceptional current, and a shared heading-reference error create different patterns across satellite position, radar ranges, visual bearings, and ship heading.
The case turns on who waived independent fixes, where the misleading agreement was displayed, and what common reference quietly biased two systems at once.

overclaim.title: No Common Satellite Shift
body: A spoofing attack should move satellite-derived position itself or create inconsistencies among receivers. The recorded satellite fixes remained smooth and matched an independent portable receiver.
The disagreement followed heading-dependent radar overlay and visual bearing, not a common displacement of every position source.

dismissal.title: The Current Was Real but Too Small
body: The measured set contributed to cross-track motion, but its integrated displacement was less than one-third of the final error.
A forecast miss does not explain the 2.8-degree heading-reference discrepancy or why fixed radar ranges rejected the displayed track.

wrongNames.title: The Error, Misassigned
body: You recognize a navigation-reference failure but place responsibility or culmination away from the officer and integrated console that turned a correctable discrepancy into a near grounding.

rounds.title: The Fleet Beyond the Horizon
rounds.connection: Three ways to move information when ships cannot rely on a physical cable.
rounds.briefing: A naval communications office can fund long-range wireless, a refined visual-signaling system, or underwater bells for fog and local coordination.
rounds.rankingCaveat: Return multipliers are pedagogical proxies for capturable program value, not audited historical investment returns.

ideas.pitch: Build high-power coastal transmitters and shipboard receivers so orders can cross hundreds or thousands of miles without a physical cable.

reveal.historicalName: Naval spark and arc radio networks
reveal.historicalOutcome: Long-range radio became a foundational fleet command-and-control system and drove a global shore-station network.
reveal.rankingRationale: It created a new operational communications layer rather than improving only one local signal method.
reveal.whyItLookedRight: Point Loma’s 1908 communication with USS Connecticut at roughly 2,900 miles showed that the core range claim was technically plausible.
reveal.returnRationale: The proxy return is high because the infrastructure served many ships and missions, though rapid technical turnover reduced the durability of any one transmitter design.

researchPackage.technicalFinding: Spark transmitters and tuned receivers can exchange Morse traffic over long distances under favorable propagation.
researchPackage.productionFinding: Coastal towers, high-power equipment, trained operators, and standardized frequencies are required.
researchPackage.adoptionFinding: A fleet gains value only when enough ships and shore stations share procedures and schedules.
researchPackage.marketContext: In 1908 the strongest market case was institutional: a navy could justify a network because each additional connected ship increased command, safety, and logistics value. Adoption depended on standard frequencies, operator training, and shore infrastructure.

ideas.pitch: Standardize searchlights, semaphore, and coded flag procedures for rapid formation-level traffic without radio emissions.

reveal.historicalOutcome: Visual signaling remained important for local fleet control and emission discipline but could not replace beyond-horizon radio.
reveal.rankingRationale: It was dependable and capturable within formations, yet its physical horizon limited strategic reach.
reveal.whyItLookedRight: Searchlights, flags, and semaphore were already proven and could be standardized with little technical risk.
reveal.returnRationale: The proxy return is moderate because implementation was inexpensive and durable, but the addressable operational problem remained local.

researchPackage.technicalFinding: Optical signals can carry coded messages reliably when ships share line of sight.
researchPackage.productionFinding: Training and standardized codebooks matter more than new industrial plant.
researchPackage.adoptionFinding: Every receiving station needs clear visibility and skilled watchstanders.
researchPackage.marketContext: Visual systems offered a low-cost, low-emission channel for nearby ships. Their adoption was easy because the equipment fit existing organizations, but weather and Earth curvature placed a hard ceiling on expansion.

ideas.pitch: Use underwater bells and hydrophones to send coded signals among ships and fixed stations when fog blocks visual methods.

reveal.historicalOutcome: Underwater bells aided navigation and signaling in some settings but did not become the fleet’s general command network.
reveal.rankingRationale: The method solved a narrow problem and was displaced by more flexible radio and sonar technologies.
reveal.whyItLookedRight: Sound can propagate through water when visibility is poor, and bells are easy to generate and detect.
reveal.returnRationale: The proxy loses capital because limited bandwidth and environmental variability constrained broad use.

researchPackage.technicalFinding: A bell produces recognizable underwater sound that a hydrophone can detect.
researchPackage.productionFinding: Fixed bells and receiving apparatus are technically simple but require local deployment.
researchPackage.adoptionFinding: Users can distinguish only a small vocabulary amid machinery and environmental noise.
researchPackage.marketContext: The concept could enter harbors and fog routes where one distinctive signal had value. It struggled to expand because complex messages and long-range coordination favored radio.

debrief.winnerReason: Radio created a scalable network whose value grew with every connected ship and station.
debrief.investorLesson: A system’s platform value can dominate a technically simpler niche solution.
debrief.roundStructureExplanation: One option creates the strongest scalable return; the concealed evidence is balanced around technical maturity versus network reach.

rounds.calibrationRationale: One option creates the strongest scalable return; the concealed evidence is balanced around technical maturity versus network reach.

rounds.title: Finding the Range in Any Weather
rounds.connection: Competing measurement channels for naval fire control.
rounds.briefing: A fleet can fund microwave radar, a major optical-director upgrade, or acoustic ranging adapted from artillery practice.
rounds.rankingCaveat: Return multipliers are pedagogical proxies for capturable program value, not audited historical investment returns.

ideas.pitch: Use radio echoes for range and bearing when darkness, haze, or target distance defeats optical observation.

reveal.historicalOutcome: Radar became central to detection and gunfire control, especially at night and in poor visibility.
reveal.rankingRationale: It expanded the conditions under which accurate range data could be generated and integrated with existing directors.
reveal.whyItLookedRight: Wartime sets demonstrated that radio echoes could provide range when optical instruments could not.
reveal.returnRationale: The proxy return is high because radar upgraded multiple mission areas, although fast model turnover imposed heavy reinvestment.

researchPackage.technicalFinding: Radar can estimate range from echo delay and bearing from antenna direction.
researchPackage.productionFinding: Shipboard antennas, transmitters, receivers, displays, maintenance, and electromagnetic integration are required.
researchPackage.adoptionFinding: Adoption is strongest where poor visibility makes existing optical ranging unreliable.
researchPackage.marketContext: By 1940 the market case rested on a concrete operational gap: optical systems lost performance at night, in haze, and at long range. A radar set could enter as an adjunct to established directors, then expand as crews trusted and maintained it.

ideas.pitch: Improve large optical rangefinders, stable directors, and mechanical rangekeepers for daylight gunnery.

reveal.historicalOutcome: Optical directors and mechanical fire-control computers remained highly capable and often worked alongside radar.
reveal.rankingRationale: They were valuable, mature systems but did not remove the visibility constraint that radar attacked.
reveal.whyItLookedRight: Long-base optical instruments and analog rangekeepers already supported accurate daylight fire control.
reveal.returnRationale: The proxy return is solid because fleets had installed bases and trained crews, but radar reduced the ceiling on further standalone growth.

researchPackage.technicalFinding: Stereoscopic or coincidence optics can estimate range from parallax with a sufficiently long baseline.
researchPackage.productionFinding: Large stable mounts, precision optics, and trained operators are required.
researchPackage.adoptionFinding: Existing ships and doctrine lower adoption friction, but weather and darkness remain external constraints.
researchPackage.marketContext: The installed base made optical improvement a rational near-term investment. Its weakness was not technical failure but a market ceiling: users still needed a different sensor when the target could not be seen.

ideas.pitch: Estimate gunfire geometry from the arrival times of muzzle blast and shell-related sound at separated microphones.

reveal.historicalOutcome: Sound ranging had important land applications but did not become the primary moving-ship fire-control solution.
reveal.rankingRationale: Atmospheric path variability and slow sound speed made it poorly matched to rapid naval fire-control updates.
reveal.whyItLookedRight: Separated microphones can locate impulsive sources from relative arrival times.
reveal.returnRationale: The proxy return is low because the physical channel was mismatched to the high-update, moving-platform problem.

researchPackage.technicalFinding: Time-difference-of-arrival can locate an impulsive sound source.
researchPackage.productionFinding: A calibrated array and atmospheric model are needed, while ship vibration and motion complicate baselines.
researchPackage.adoptionFinding: The likely adopters are fixed shore systems rather than maneuvering ships requiring rapid continuous range updates.
researchPackage.marketContext: The method had a credible physical demonstration but a weak fit to moving naval platforms. A fixed user could tolerate calibration and delay; a gunnery director needed faster, more stable updates.

debrief.winnerReason: Radar removed the visibility constraint while integrating with the director and range-keeper ecosystem.
debrief.investorLesson: The best system often complements installed machinery before it replaces it.
debrief.roundStructureExplanation: Radar and optical systems both create value, but radar’s realized excess return is larger because it opens night and poor-visibility operations.

rounds.calibrationRationale: Radar and optical systems both create value, but radar’s realized excess return is larger because it opens night and poor-visibility operations.

rounds.title: A Position Anywhere at Sea
rounds.connection: Three architectures for accurate position across long deployments.
rounds.briefing: A navigation program can invest in a satellite Doppler system, a terrestrial hyperbolic radio chain, or self-contained inertial navigation.
rounds.rankingCaveat: Return multipliers are pedagogical proxies for capturable program value, not audited historical investment returns.

ideas.pitch: Infer position from the changing frequency of signals from precisely tracked low-Earth-orbit satellites.

reveal.historicalOutcome: Transit became the first operational satellite navigation system and supported Navy navigation and geodesy before GPS replaced it.
reveal.rankingRationale: It demonstrated a global infrastructure model and directly served high-value naval users.
reveal.whyItLookedRight: The Doppler shift of a known satellite signal can constrain receiver position when the satellite orbit is accurately known.
reveal.returnRationale: The proxy return is high because the system created a new global service, though later GPS limited its long-term monopoly.

researchPackage.technicalFinding: Measured Doppler shift over a satellite pass can yield a position fix from a known orbit.
researchPackage.productionFinding: A constellation, tracking network, timing, orbit determination, and receivers are required.
researchPackage.adoptionFinding: High-value naval and surveying users can justify sparse fixes before mass-market receivers exist.
researchPackage.marketContext: In 1960 the first adopters valued global reach more than continuous updates. Submarines and surveyors could tolerate scheduled passes because alternatives accumulated error or depended on regional transmitters.

ideas.pitch: Use synchronized shore transmitters and signal-time differences to create lines of position over large ocean regions.

reveal.historicalOutcome: LORAN-C provided long-range regional navigation for military and civilian users for decades.
reveal.rankingRationale: It delivered large practical value with mature terrestrial infrastructure but never achieved truly global autonomous coverage.
reveal.whyItLookedRight: Time differences from synchronized transmitters define hyperbolic lines of position.
reveal.returnRationale: The proxy return is strong because shore infrastructure served many users and persisted for decades.

researchPackage.technicalFinding: Stable low-frequency signals from synchronized transmitters support repeatable time-difference navigation.
researchPackage.productionFinding: Chains of surveyed transmitters and continuous maintenance are required.
researchPackage.adoptionFinding: Receivers are useful wherever a chain covers the route; benefits scale regionally rather than globally.
researchPackage.marketContext: The market case was strong in heavily traveled regions because one shore chain could serve many ships and aircraft. Expansion slowed where geography or politics made transmitter sites difficult.

ideas.pitch: Integrate gyroscope and accelerometer measurements to estimate motion without external emissions or radio reception.

reveal.historicalOutcome: Inertial navigation became essential for submarines, missiles, aircraft, and ships, usually aided by external fixes.
reveal.rankingRationale: Its autonomy was uniquely valuable, but accumulated drift made it a complement rather than a complete global reference.
reveal.whyItLookedRight: Gyroscopes and accelerometers can propagate position continuously from a known initial state.
reveal.returnRationale: The proxy return is strong because high-value platforms paid for autonomy, though precision hardware and aiding requirements limited broad early adoption.

researchPackage.technicalFinding: An inertial unit measures rotation and acceleration without receiving an external signal.
researchPackage.productionFinding: Precision sensors, stable platforms, calibration, and computing are required.
researchPackage.adoptionFinding: Submarines and strategic systems value continuous silent operation enough to absorb high cost.
researchPackage.marketContext: The initial market was narrow but valuable: platforms that could not expose antennas or depend on regional transmitters. Adoption expanded as sensor cost fell and external aiding became easier.

debrief.winnerReason: Transit built the new global service model, while LORAN-C and inertial navigation also delivered durable value.
debrief.investorLesson: Multiple systems can succeed because they solve different coverage, autonomy, and update-rate constraints.
debrief.roundStructureExplanation: All three beat cash in the pedagogical model; the benchmark spreads capital across global reach, regional infrastructure, and autonomous continuity in proportion to realized excess returns.

rounds.calibrationRationale: All three beat cash in the pedagogical model; the benchmark spreads capital across global reach, regional infrastructure, and autonomous continuity in proportion to realized excess returns.

Protocol.title: The Uncorrelated Contact
Protocol.mission: A contact appears near a busy strait. Match each information need to the instrument or system that supplies the required observable without assuming any single sensor proves identity.
briefing: Range and bearing must be maintained through haze.
Cooperative identity may be absent or misleading.
Radio-frequency emissions can reveal equipment without yielding visual identity.
A submerged or slow contact may require a different physical channel.
Protocol.takeaway: Contact identification is an evidence-fusion problem: geometry, cooperative data, imagery, emissions, acoustics, and motion answer different questions.

events.title: Maintain range and bearing
events.text: The team needs repeated all-weather measurements of surface-contact range and azimuth over tens of nautical miles, including at night.
events.why: Surface-search radar measures range from echo delay and bearing from antenna direction through darkness and moderate haze.

events.title: Check cooperative identity
events.text: The contact may be broadcasting a vessel name, position, course, and speed. The team needs the standardized self-report, not an independent physical measurement.
events.why: AIS receives cooperative identity and navigation messages; it is useful evidence but can be absent or incorrect.

events.title: Inspect visible structure
events.text: At shorter range, analysts need mast, hull, deck-load, and light-pattern details with human-interpretable imagery.
events.why: A stabilized electro-optical camera provides daylight imagery and angular detail for visual comparison.

events.title: See through darkness
events.text: The hull is warm against a cool night background, but visible illumination is poor. The team needs passive thermal contrast.
events.why: A mid- or long-wave infrared imager maps emitted thermal radiation without illuminating the contact.

events.title: Characterize radio emissions
events.text: The contact transmits intermittently. Analysts need frequency, pulse structure, direction of arrival, and emitter-library comparison without sending a radar pulse.
events.why: Electronic-support measures intercept and characterize external radio-frequency emissions passively.

events.title: Measure underwater sound
events.text: A low-frequency tonal persists when the surface radar loses the contact behind land clutter. The team needs bearing to machinery and propeller noise.
events.why: A passive hydrophone array measures underwater pressure signals and beamforms them for acoustic bearing and spectrum.

events.title: Test motion consistency
events.text: The bridge needs closest point of approach and time to closest point using a history of ranges and bearings rather than one snapshot.
events.why: Automatic radar plotting aid uses successive radar measurements to estimate relative motion, CPA, and TCPA.

cards.name: Surface-search radar
cards.spec: Provides repeated range and bearing from radio echoes; works without contact cooperation and supports tracking.

cards.name: Automatic Identification System receiver
cards.spec: Receives standardized cooperative vessel identity, position, course, and speed reports.

cards.name: Stabilized daylight electro-optical camera
cards.spec: Provides magnified visible imagery for hull, mast, markings, lights, and deck configuration.

cards.name: Thermal infrared imager
cards.spec: Provides passive imagery from emitted heat, especially useful at night or against thermal contrast.

cards.name: Electronic-support measures suite
cards.spec: Passively detects radio-frequency emissions and estimates frequency, waveform features, and direction of arrival.

cards.name: Passive hydrophone array
cards.spec: Receives underwater sound and estimates acoustic bearing and spectral features without transmitting.

cards.name: Automatic radar plotting aid
cards.spec: Uses a sequence of radar plots to estimate contact course, speed, CPA, and TCPA.

cards.name: Meteorological radar
cards.spec: Maps precipitation and weather cells; it is not optimized for identifying a nearby vessel or analyzing its emissions.

cards.name: Hull-mounted echo sounder
cards.spec: Measures water depth beneath the ship from two-way acoustic travel time, not a surface contact’s identity.

cards.name: Magnetic compass
cards.spec: Provides own-ship heading relative to magnetic north; it does not measure another contact’s range or emissions.

Protocol.title: Smoke in the Motor Controller Room
Protocol.domain: Damage control · Fire science · Electrical safety
Protocol.mission: A shipboard electrical fire produces smoke in an enclosed equipment room. Match each stage to the tool or system whose physical function fits the information and hazard at that moment.
briefing: Power may continue feeding an electrical fault.
Opening the space can add oxygen and spread smoke.
Water fog is valuable for cooling, but energized equipment changes the risk.
A post-fire space can retain toxic gases and hidden heat.
Protocol.takeaway: Successful firefighting separates detection, electrical isolation, boundary control, attack, atmospheric protection, thermal verification, and re-entry monitoring.

events.title: Confirm the alarm location
events.text: Smoke detection has activated, but the team needs to identify which enclosed zone has obscuration before opening doors.
events.why: An addressable smoke-detection panel identifies the alarming detector and zone while the space remains closed.

events.title: Remove electrical energy
events.text: The suspected fault is in a motor controller. The team must de-energize the specific feeder and prevent inadvertent re-energization.
events.why: Remote breaker operation plus lockout/tagout removes the electrical source and controls restoration.

events.title: Protect adjacent spaces
events.text: Steel boundaries are heating. The team needs to limit heat transfer and watch for fire spread without feeding air into the compartment.
events.why: A charged hose team cools exposed boundaries from the safe side and checks adjacent compartments.

events.title: Enter contaminated air
events.text: Smoke and combustion products make the atmosphere immediately dangerous to life and health. Firefighters require an independent breathing supply.
events.why: Self-contained breathing apparatus supplies breathable air independent of the compartment atmosphere.

events.title: Attack the seat of fire
events.text: Electrical isolation is confirmed. The team needs a controllable stream that cools burning insulation and nearby structure while limiting steam production.
events.why: A naval water-fog applicator provides cooling and fine droplets after electrical isolation is established.

events.title: Find hidden hot spots
events.text: Visible flame is out, but cable trays and panel backs may retain heat behind covers. The team needs a non-contact temperature map.
events.why: A thermal imager reveals hot components and heat patterns that are not obvious in visible smoke or darkness.

events.title: Verify atmosphere before restoration
events.text: Before ventilation changes and unprotected re-entry, the team needs oxygen, flammable-vapor, and toxic-gas measurements.
events.why: A calibrated multi-gas meter checks oxygen concentration, combustible gas, carbon monoxide, and hydrogen sulfide.

cards.name: Addressable smoke-detection panel
cards.spec: Identifies the detector and zone producing the alarm without requiring immediate entry.

cards.name: Remote breaker control and lockout/tagout kit
cards.spec: De-energizes a selected feeder and prevents unauthorized restoration while work continues.

cards.name: Boundary-cooling hose team
cards.spec: Applies cooling from adjacent spaces and monitors bulkheads and decks for fire spread.

cards.name: Self-contained breathing apparatus
cards.spec: Supplies independent breathing air in smoke, oxygen-deficient, or toxic atmospheres.

cards.name: Water-fog applicator
cards.spec: Produces fine droplets for cooling and fire suppression once electrical conditions permit.

cards.name: Thermal imaging camera
cards.spec: Maps surface-temperature differences to locate hot spots through darkness and residual smoke.

cards.name: Calibrated four-gas meter
cards.spec: Measures oxygen, flammability, carbon monoxide, and hydrogen sulfide before re-entry or restoration.

cards.name: Aqueous-film-forming foam eductor
cards.spec: Proportions foam for flammable-liquid surface fires; it is not the primary tool for an isolated electrical cabinet after power removal.

cards.name: Radiation survey meter
cards.spec: Measures ionizing radiation and does not determine smoke location, electrical isolation, or combustion gases.

cards.name: Salinity meter
cards.spec: Measures dissolved salts in water and does not locate hidden heat or verify a breathable atmosphere.

Protocol.title: Restore the Split Plant
Protocol.mission: A fault trips one ship-service bus and several loads go dark. Match each restoration stage to the instrument or system that provides the needed isolation, verification, or controlled re-energization.
briefing: Protection operated for a reason; immediate reclosure may feed the fault again.
Voltage absence must be verified before touching conductors.
Emergency loads have priority over hotel loads.
Parallel sources require phase, frequency, and voltage agreement.
Protocol.takeaway: Electrical restoration is a controlled diagnostic sequence: read protection, isolate, prove dead, test, energize a healthy section, synchronize sources, and add load gradually.

events.title: Read the protection record
events.text: The team needs to know which breaker opened first and whether overcurrent, ground fault, or differential protection asserted.
events.why: A protective-relay event record provides trip elements, timestamps, and current or voltage snapshots.

events.title: Separate the suspected section
events.text: A feeder cable may be damaged. The team must establish visible and electrically secure isolation before testing.
events.why: A disconnect and lockout/tagout arrangement creates a controlled isolation boundary.

events.title: Prove conductors de-energized
events.text: Before insulation testing, technicians must verify absence of voltage on each phase with a device proven before and after use.
events.why: An appropriately rated voltage detector verifies that the isolated conductors are de-energized.

events.title: Test cable insulation
events.text: The feeder is isolated and dead. The team needs resistance under a controlled DC test voltage to detect degraded insulation to ground.
events.why: A megohmmeter applies a specified DC voltage and measures high insulation resistance.

events.title: Energize the healthy bus section
events.text: A standby generator is running, but its breaker remains open. Operators need bus and generator voltage before considering closure.
events.why: Switchboard metering displays source and bus voltage, frequency, current, and breaker status.

events.title: Match an incoming generator
events.text: Before paralleling, the incoming source must match bus phase sequence, phase angle, frequency, and voltage.
events.why: A synchroscope and synchronizing lamps indicate relative phase and frequency for safe breaker closure.

events.title: Restore loads by priority
events.text: After the healthy bus is energized, loads must return in controlled blocks while current and frequency remain within limits.
events.why: The load-shed and distribution console restores priority groups and monitors generator loading.

cards.name: Protective-relay event recorder
cards.spec: Stores trip elements, timestamps, and electrical waveforms showing how protection operated.

cards.name: Breaker–disconnect isolation and lockout/tagout boundary
cards.spec: Opens the interrupting device, establishes visible separation where fitted, and controls every energy source to the suspect feeder.

cards.name: Rated voltage detector
cards.spec: Verifies absence of voltage with a live-dead-live check before contact work or insulation testing.

cards.name: Insulation-resistance tester
cards.spec: Applies a controlled DC test voltage to measure resistance between conductors and ground.

cards.name: Main switchboard metering
cards.spec: Displays source and bus voltage, frequency, current, power, and breaker condition.

cards.name: Synchroscope and synchronizing lamps
cards.spec: Shows phase-angle and frequency difference between an incoming generator and an energized bus.

cards.name: Automatic load-shed and restoration console
cards.spec: Sequences priority loads and watches generator limits during restoration.

cards.name: Pipe clamp thermometer
cards.spec: Measures pipe-surface temperature and does not identify relay trips or establish electrical synchronization.

cards.name: Ventilation anemometer
cards.spec: Measures air speed in ducts and does not verify conductor voltage or insulation resistance.

cards.name: Navigation echo sounder
cards.spec: Measures depth below the keel and has no role in ship-service bus restoration.

Protocol.title: Fuel Across the Gap
Protocol.mission: Two ships conduct a connected replenishment at sea. Match each stage to the equipment whose mechanical or informational role fits that point in the evolution.
briefing: The ships must maintain a stable relative course and separation.
A light messenger crosses before any heavy transfer rig.
The fuel hose needs independent support and emergency release.
Pressure and tank level must be monitored throughout transfer.
Protocol.takeaway: Underway replenishment is a staged load path: station keeping, communications, messenger transfer, rig tensioning, hose connection, monitored pumping, and emergency breakaway readiness.

events.title: Hold relative station
events.text: The receiving ship must maintain prescribed lateral separation and fore-aft position while both ships move through the water.
events.why: Bridge-to-bridge station-keeping uses course, speed, visual references, and relative-position reports.

events.title: Establish dedicated coordination
events.text: Rig teams need a continuous voice circuit independent of hand signals and general tactical radio traffic.
events.why: A sound-powered phone circuit provides dedicated local communications without external electrical power.

events.title: Send the first light line
events.text: The gap is too wide and dangerous for personnel to pass a heavy cable directly. A lightweight line must carry progressively heavier messengers.
events.why: A line-throwing device sends a light shot line that can haul over messenger and span-wire components.

events.title: Support the transfer rig
events.text: The span wire must remain under controlled tension as ships heave and separate, without becoming rigid or going slack.
events.why: A constant-tension ram compensates for relative motion while supporting the rig.

events.title: Connect the fuel hose
events.text: The receiving station needs a standardized coupling that can be secured, inspected, and rapidly released.
events.why: A probe-and-receiver fuel fitting makes the controlled hose connection between ships.

events.title: Monitor transfer
events.text: Operators need delivery pressure, flow rate, and receiving-tank level so pumping can stop before overpressure or overflow.
events.why: The fuel-transfer console integrates pump status, pressure, flow, valve lineup, and tank sounding.

events.title: Prepare emergency separation
events.text: If station keeping is lost, the rig must be released in a planned order without dragging hoses or parting loaded lines unpredictably.
events.why: The emergency breakaway controls and procedures release transfer components in a controlled sequence.

cards.name: Bridge station-keeping team
cards.spec: Maintains relative course, speed, separation, and fore-aft position using visual and instrument references.

cards.name: Sound-powered telephone circuit
cards.spec: Provides a dedicated local voice path that does not depend on ship service power.

cards.name: Pneumatic line-throwing device
cards.spec: Projects a light line across the gap so progressively heavier messenger lines can follow.

cards.name: Constant-tension ram
cards.spec: Adjusts payout to maintain span-wire tension despite heave and small separation changes.

cards.name: Fuel probe-and-receiver coupling
cards.spec: Creates a standardized, inspectable, and releasable connection for the transfer hose.

cards.name: Fuel-transfer monitoring console
cards.spec: Displays pump, pressure, flow, valve, and tank-level information during delivery.

cards.name: Emergency breakaway control panel
cards.spec: Supports rapid, ordered release of the rig when safe station cannot be maintained.

cards.name: Marine sextant
cards.spec: Measures celestial or horizontal angles for navigation, not line transfer or hose support between nearby ships.

cards.name: Air-deployed sonobuoy
cards.spec: Measures underwater acoustic conditions and does not maintain replenishment rig tension.

cards.name: Firefighting foam monitor
cards.spec: Projects foam onto a fuel fire; it is contingency equipment, not the primary system for routine hose connection or transfer measurement.
